title: Anointing, Last Supper, Gethsemane, and Arrest
summary: Two days before Passover the chief priests and elders plot Jesus' death, a woman anoints him at Bethany, and Judas agrees to hand him over for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus shares the Passover meal with the Twelve, giving them bread and cup as his body and his blood of the covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins, then prays in anguish in Gethsemane while the disciples sleep. He is arrested and abandoned, and before Caiaphas and the council he is condemned for blasphemy, while in the courtyard Peter three times denies knowing him.
story:
Jesus has finished his teaching. Verse 1 uses the formula that closes each of Matthew's five great discourses, but with a difference: this time Jesus has finished all these sayings, and there will be no more speeches. The passion begins at once, and Jesus himself announces it (verse 2). Everything he predicted on the road to Jerusalem (16:21, 17:22-23, 20:18-19) now happens in quick succession, and the verb of those predictions, to hand over, runs through the chapter like a drumbeat.

The chapter sets devotion beside betrayal and faithfulness beside failure. An unnamed woman spends a fortune on Jesus while one of the Twelve sells him for a slave's price. Jesus gives himself to his disciples in bread and cup, and hours later they all desert him. He holds firm in prayer while his closest friends sleep, and he confesses the truth under oath before the high priest while Peter, outside, swears that he does not know him. The chapter ends with Jesus condemned by Israel's highest court and Peter weeping in the dark. Chapter 27 brings the Roman trial, the cross, and the burial.
historical:
Passover (Hebrew pesach, Greek pascha) remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 12). The lambs were slaughtered in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, in March or April, and eaten that night, which by Jewish reckoning was already 15 Nisan, and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread followed (Leviticus 23:5-8). By the first century the two names were used for the whole festival, which is why verse 17 can call the day the lambs were killed the first day of Unleavened Bread. Pilgrims crowded into Jerusalem, and a feast of liberation under Roman rule made the city tense. Josephus tells of a riot at Passover under the governor Cumanus, around AD 48 to 52, in which many were crushed to death (Jewish War 2.224-227), which explains the leaders' fear in verse 5 of an uproar among the people.

Matthew alone names the high priest, and names him twice (verses 3 and 57). Joseph called Caiaphas was appointed by the prefect Valerius Gratus around AD 18 and removed by the Syrian legate Vitellius around 36 or 37 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.35, 18.95). His long tenure overlapped almost exactly with Pilate's (about 26 to 36), which implies a working relationship with Rome. In 1990 a family tomb in south Jerusalem yielded an ornate ossuary inscribed with the name Joseph son of Caiaphas, which many scholars identify as his. The Sanhedrin (verse 59) was Jerusalem's supreme council of chief priests, elders, and scribes, presided over by the high priest. Under the Roman prefects it handled religious and many civil matters, but according to John 18:31 it could not carry out a death sentence on its own authority, which is why the case goes to Pilate in the morning (27:1-2).

Whether the night hearing was lawful is an old question. The Mishnah's tractate Sanhedrin, compiled around AD 200, requires capital cases to be tried by day and forbids them on the eve of a Sabbath or festival (m. Sanhedrin 4:1), voids testimony when witnesses contradict each other (5:2), and defines blasphemy narrowly as pronouncing the divine name (7:5). Jewish scholars such as Joseph Klausner (Jesus of Nazareth, English 1925), Paul Winter (On the Trial of Jesus, 1961), and Haim Cohn (The Trial and Death of Jesus) argued that a Jewish court would not have acted as the Gospels describe and that responsibility lay mainly with Rome and a few collaborating priests. Herbert Danby (1919) and Raymond Brown (The Death of the Messiah, 1994) replied that the Mishnah records the idealized law of the rabbis after AD 70, not the practice of a Sadducean priestly council in the 30s. Matthew himself presents a proceeding whose verdict was settled in advance (verses 4 and 59) and shows that even by the court's own standard the witnesses failed until two agreed (verses 60-61, compare Deuteronomy 19:15). Outside the New Testament, Josephus's paragraph on Jesus, though later expanded by Christian copyists, is widely thought to have said originally that Pilate condemned him on the accusation of leading men among the Jews (Antiquities 18.63-64).

Thirty pieces of silver (verse 15) were most likely shekels of Tyre, the heavy silver coins in which the temple tax had to be paid and which the chief priests would have had on hand. Matthew alone gives the amount, and his verb, they weighed out or set out (estēsan), is the verb of the Greek text of Zechariah 11:12, where the shepherd's wages are weighed out as thirty pieces of silver. Gethsemane, Aramaic for oil press, was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives across the Kidron from the temple; the Church of All Nations, completed in 1924, stands over the traditional site. A Roman legion (verse 53) numbered about five to six thousand men, so twelve legions of angels would be an army of some sixty thousand or more.
cultural:
Guests at a festive meal reclined on couches or cushions, leaning on the left elbow, and the Mishnah requires even the poorest Israelite to recline at Passover as a sign of freedom (m. Pesachim 10:1). The meal followed an order that the Mishnah describes in its final form (m. Pesachim 10): blessings over cups of wine, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, a dish of sauce into which food was dipped (verse 23), the roasted lamb, a son's questions, the father's retelling of the exodus, and the singing of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113 to 118). Rabban Gamaliel is remembered as teaching that whoever has not explained the lamb, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs has not fulfilled the duty (m. Pesachim 10:5). How much of this order was fixed in Jesus' day is debated, but a host interpreting the food of the meal is exactly what Jesus does. Before breaking bread a Jewish host spoke a blessing to God, the traditional form praising him as the one who brings forth bread from the earth (m. Berakhot 6:1), and a cup over which thanks was said was called the cup of blessing, the phrase Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 10:16. The hymn of verse 30 was most likely the second half of the Hallel, Psalms 115 to 118, which ends with the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22), a psalm Jesus had quoted days earlier (21:42).

The anointing at Bethany involved a household treasure. Perfume was stored in a flask of alabaster, a soft translucent stone, with a long neck that could be broken to pour out the contents. Anointing a guest's head with oil was an act of honor (Psalm 23:5), and the anointing of a head also recalled how prophets anointed kings (1 Samuel 10:1, 2 Kings 9:6), while anointing a body belonged to burial. Simon the Leper was presumably known by a disease he no longer had, since a man with active skin disease could not host a dinner. Almsgiving to the poor was expected at Passover, which is why the disciples' objection sounded pious (compare John 13:29).

Disciples greeted their teacher with a kiss, which made Judas's signal both inconspicuous and monstrous, and Rabbi, literally my great one, was a respectful address for a teacher. When the high priest says, I charge You under oath by the living God (verse 63), he uses a formula of adjuration that obliged a person to answer; Leviticus 5:1 makes it a sin for a witness who hears such a public charge to stay silent, which may be why Jesus, silent until then, now speaks. Tearing one's garments was a sign of grief or horror, and the Mishnah later requires judges who hear blasphemy to tear their clothes (m. Sanhedrin 7:5). Spitting in the face and striking were gestures of utter contempt (Numbers 12:14, Isaiah 50:6). Galileans spoke Aramaic with a recognizable accent; the Babylonian Talmud preserves jokes about Galileans who could not keep their guttural letters apart (b. Eruvin 53b), which is what gives Peter away (verse 73). The rooster's crow marked the last watch before dawn, and though the Mishnah says chickens were not to be raised in Jerusalem (m. Bava Kamma 7:7), the rule may not have been kept.
literary:
Matthew follows Mark's order closely in this chapter, and the details he adds show his concerns. He opens with Jesus himself announcing the passion (verses 1-2), so that the plot of the leaders in verse 3 follows Jesus' own word rather than taking him by surprise. He gives the price of the betrayal, thirty pieces of silver, preparing for the fulfillment of Zechariah in 27:9-10. At the supper he has Judas ask, like the others, Surely not I, but where they say Lord, Judas says Rabbi (verses 22 and 25), the address he uses again at the kiss (verse 49); in Matthew no disciple but Judas ever addresses Jesus as teacher or rabbi. He adds that Jesus answered Judas, You have said it yourself, the same answer Jesus gives Caiaphas (verse 64) and Pilate (27:11). To the cup word he adds the command, Drink from it, all of you, and the phrase for the forgiveness of sins (verses 27-28). In Gethsemane he gives the words of the second prayer, which repeat the Lord's Prayer exactly, may Your will be done (verse 42, compare 6:10). At the arrest he adds Jesus' address, Friend, the rebuke of the sword, and the twelve legions (verses 50-54).

The chapter is built from contrasts. The leaders' plot (3-5) and Judas's bargain (14-16) frame the woman's extravagant act (6-13). At the supper the announcement of betrayal is set beside the gift of bread and cup. In Gethsemane Jesus prays three times while the disciples sleep three times; in the courtyard Peter denies him three times, and each denial is sharper than the last, from evasion (verse 70) to an oath (72) to cursing and swearing (74). Peter's oath breaks Jesus' teaching that his disciples should not swear at all (5:33-37), while Jesus, placed under oath, tells the truth. The trial inside and the denial outside happen at the same time, and Matthew cuts between them so that the reader watches both. Throughout, the language of Scripture and fulfillment (verses 24, 31, 54, 56) insists that none of this is accident, and the chapter ends not with Jesus but with Peter remembering Jesus' word and weeping, the last time Matthew shows him.

doctrines.note: Jesus interprets his coming death as blood poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (verse 28). The words gather Exodus 24:8, where covenant blood binds Israel to God, and Isaiah 53:12, where the servant pours out his life and bears the sin of many, and Matthew moves the phrase for the forgiveness of sins here from John's baptism (Mark 1:4, compare Matthew 3:2), so that forgiveness is tied to Jesus' death.

My blood of the covenant (verse 28) presents Jesus' death as the sacrifice that establishes a covenant between God and his people, as the blood Moses sprinkled did at Sinai. Paul's and Luke's form of the words, the new covenant in my blood (1 Corinthians 11:25, Luke 22:20), makes explicit the link with Jeremiah 31:31-34, where the new covenant brings the forgiveness of sins.

The Lord's Supper is instituted here, and Christians have celebrated it ever since. Traditions differ on how Christ is present in it (a change of the bread and wine into his body and blood, a real presence with the elements, a spiritual presence received by faith, or a memorial), but all receive it as Jesus' own gift binding his people to his death and to the coming kingdom (verse 29).

In Gethsemane Jesus prays with complete honesty for the cup to pass and then submits, not as I will, but as You will (verse 39). His second prayer repeats the Lord's Prayer, may Your will be done (verse 42, compare 6:10), and his warning to watch and pray so as not to enter into temptation echoes its petition, lead us not into temptation (6:13).

The Son of Man goes just as it is written, yet woe to the one who betrays him (verse 24). Jesus could call twelve legions of angels but will not, so that the Scriptures are fulfilled (verses 53-54). Human plotting, betrayal, and cowardice are real and culpable, and God works his purpose through the very acts that oppose it without excusing those who commit them.

words.note: Diathēkē, covenant. It occurs thirty-three times in the New Testament, seventeen of them in Hebrews, and only here in Matthew. In ordinary Greek it meant a last will or testament, which is why older English Bibles speak of the new testament; the Greek Old Testament chose it to translate the Hebrew berit, God's binding commitment to his people, perhaps because a will is set by one party. At Sinai Moses sprinkled blood and called it the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8), and Jesus uses the same words of his own blood.

Aphesis, release, forgiveness. It occurs seventeen times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and Acts, and only here in Matthew. In the Greek Old Testament it names the release of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10), and in Luke 4:18 it describes liberty for captives. BDAG gives both senses, release from bondage and pardon of sin. Matthew, who omitted the phrase for the forgiveness of sins from his account of John's baptism, places it here, attached to Jesus' blood.

Potērion, cup. It occurs thirty-one times in the New Testament and seven in Matthew. At the supper it is the cup of the covenant (verse 27); in Gethsemane it is the cup Jesus asks to pass from him (verses 39 and 42), the same cup he told James and John they would drink (20:22-23). In the prophets the cup often stands for God's judgment poured out on sin (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15-16), which helps explain the depth of Jesus' anguish.

Pascha, Passover, a Greek form of the Aramaic name of the festival. It occurs twenty-nine times in the New Testament and four times in this chapter (verses 2, 17, 18, 19). It can mean the festival, the lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7, Christ our Passover lamb), or the meal. Matthew presents the supper as a Passover meal, so that Jesus interprets his death through the exodus deliverance, the foundational act of salvation in Israel's story.

Paradidōmi, to hand over, deliver up, betray. It occurs about 120 times in the New Testament and runs through Matthew's passion predictions (17:22, 20:18-19, 26:2). In this chapter Judas hands him over (verses 15, 16, 21, 23, 24, 25, 46, 48), in the next the council hands him over to Pilate (27:2) and Pilate hands him over to be crucified (27:26). The same verb is used in the Greek of Isaiah 53:6 and 53:12 for the servant given up for sins, and Paul uses it of the Father who handed over his Son for us all (Romans 8:32). William Klassen (1996) argued that it never means betray in itself, a point most lexicons grant while noting that context gives it that sense here.

Hetairos, companion, friend. It occurs only three times in the New Testament, all in Matthew, and each time as an address to someone in the wrong: the grumbling laborer (20:13), the guest without a wedding garment (22:12), and Judas (26:50). It is not the warm word for friend (philos) but a polite, distancing address, something like my good man. The words that follow, eph' ho parei, are compressed and can be read as a command, do what you came for, or as a question, why are you here, which older versions follow.

Aparneomai, to deny, disown. It occurs eleven times in the New Testament and four times in Matthew. Jesus used it when he said that anyone who would come after him must deny himself (16:24), and he uses it of Peter's coming failure (verses 34 and 35); verse 75 repeats it. Peter, who would not deny himself, denies his Lord. The related verb arneomai, used in verses 70 and 72, recalls Jesus' warning that whoever denies him before others he will deny before his Father (10:33).

Peirasmos, testing, temptation. It occurs about twenty times in the New Testament and twice in Matthew: in the Lord's Prayer, lead us not into temptation (6:13), and in Gethsemane, watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation (26:41). The word covers both trial from outside and enticement to sin; here it names the hour of pressure that is about to scatter the disciples. Jesus, who was tested in the wilderness (4:1, the verb peirazō), faces the decisive test in prayer while his friends sleep.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the one who knowingly gives himself up. He announces his handing over before anyone plots it (verse 2). He accepts the woman's anointing as preparation for his burial (verse 12), and the anointed one, the Messiah, is anointed for death. At the supper he interprets his death in advance: the bread is his body and the cup his blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. The words gather the great sacrificial moments of Israel's story: the Passover lamb whose blood marked the houses of the redeemed (Exodus 12), the covenant blood Moses sprinkled on the people at Sinai (Exodus 24:8), the servant of Isaiah who poured out his life unto death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and the new covenant in which God promises to forgive iniquity and remember sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Matthew's Gospel began with the angel's promise that Jesus would save his people from their sins (1:21); here Jesus says how.

In Gethsemane he is truly human. His soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death, words that echo the refrain of Psalms 42 and 43, and he asks three times for the cup to pass. He is also truly the Son, praying My Father, and submitting his will to the Father's; the church later confessed from this scene that Christ has a human will as well as a divine one, the human freely yielding to the divine (the Third Council of Constantinople, 681). At the arrest he refuses both the sword and the angels: the one who could command twelve legions goes to the cross because the Scriptures must be fulfilled. He is the stricken Shepherd of Zechariah 13:7, whose sheep scatter, and the shepherd who promises to go before them into Galilee after he is raised (verse 32).

Before the high priest, charged by the living God to say whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, the very confession Peter made at Caesarea Philippi (16:16), Jesus answers, You have said it yourself, and adds that from now on they will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. He joins Psalm 110:1, where David's Lord sits at God's right hand, to Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to receive everlasting dominion. The prisoner claims to be the judge. The church confesses from this chapter that his death was voluntary and given for many, that he is truly human in his sorrow and truly the Son in his claim, and that he meant his people to remember him at his table until he drinks the cup new with them in his Father's kingdom.
interpretation:
Each scene of the chapter has its own long history. The woman at Bethany, unnamed in Matthew and Mark, is Mary of Bethany in John 12:1-8. Gregory the Great (Homily 33 on the Gospels, 591) merged Mary of Bethany, Mary Magdalene, and the sinful woman of Luke 7 into one penitent figure, a reading that shaped Western art and devotion for a thousand years and that modern Catholic scholarship and the 1969 Roman calendar no longer follow. Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza took the title of her book In Memory of Her (1983) from verse 13, arguing that the church kept the memory of Judas and Peter but forgot the woman Jesus promised would be remembered.

Judas became Christianity's figure of treachery. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.31.1, around 180) mentions a Gospel of Judas used by a Gnostic group, and a Coptic Gospel of Judas from the Codex Tchacos, published in 2006, presents Judas as the one disciple who understood Jesus. Dante places Judas in the central mouth of Lucifer at the bottom of hell (Inferno 34). The Jewish scholar Hyam Maccoby (Judas Iscariot and the Myth of Jewish Evil, 1992) traced how Judas, whose name echoes Judah and Judaeus, became a symbol through which Christians portrayed the Jewish people as betrayers. Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942) gave Judas a long theological treatment as the rejected one for whom Christ was also handed over, and William Klassen (Judas: Betrayer or Friend of Jesus?, 1996) argued that the earliest sources did not portray him as a traitor.

The words over the bread and cup became the center of Christian worship and of its fiercest debates. The Didache (9-10) gives early eucharistic prayers, Ignatius of Antioch around 110 calls the Eucharist the flesh of Christ (To the Smyrnaeans 7.1), and Justin Martyr around 155 describes the Sunday Eucharist (First Apology 66-67). The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) used the term transubstantiation. At the Marburg Colloquy (1529) Luther insisted on the plain sense of this is my body and Zwingli read it as signifies, and the two could not agree; Calvin taught a real spiritual feeding on Christ by faith, and the Council of Trent (1551) reaffirmed transubstantiation. The ecumenical Lima document Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982) recorded how far the churches had come toward common understanding. Tertullian (On Idolatry 19) read Jesus' rebuke of the sword in verse 52 as disarming every Christian soldier, a key text in early Christian nonviolence and in later pacifist traditions, while Augustine and most later theologians read it as forbidding private violence rather than all use of force by rulers. Maximus the Confessor made Gethsemane central to the doctrine of Christ's two wills, confessed at the Third Council of Constantinople (681).

In art, Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper (1495 to 1498, Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan) captures the moment of verse 21, Giotto's Kiss of Judas in the Scrovegni Chapel (about 1305) and Caravaggio's Taking of Christ (1602, rediscovered in Dublin in 1990) show the arrest, and Andrea Mantegna's Agony in the Garden (about 1458 to 1460, National Gallery, London) shows the sleeping disciples. J. S. Bach's St Matthew Passion (Leipzig, 1727) sets Matthew 26 and 27 in full; the alto aria Erbarme dich follows Peter's bitter weeping. The Church of Saint Peter in Gallicantu (1931) in Jerusalem commemorates the denial. The Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read Matthew 26:14 to 27:66 on Palm or Passion Sunday in Year A, and the words of institution are said at every celebration of the Eucharist.
text:
A few manuscript differences show in English Bibles. In verse 28 later manuscripts, including Codex Alexandrinus and the Byzantine text followed by the King James Version, read ‘blood of the new testament’; the earliest witnesses, among them Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack ‘new’, which was probably added from Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. In verse 3 the King James Version adds ‘and the scribes’ with later manuscripts. Luke's verses about the angel and the sweat like drops of blood (Luke 22:43-44) are placed after Matthew 26:39 in the manuscripts of family 13 and in some lectionaries, a sign of how the Holy Week readings were combined. The fragments of Matthew 26 in P64 and P67 (Oxford and Barcelona, around AD 200) are among the earliest surviving pieces of the Gospel.

Translation differences are more visible. In verse 45 the Greek can be read as a command or a question: ‘Sleep on now, and take your rest’ (KJV) or ‘Are you still sleeping and resting?’ (BSB, NIV). In verse 50 the compressed phrase eph' ho parei is rendered as a question, ‘wherefore art thou come?’ (KJV), or as a command, ‘do what you came for’ (BSB, ESV, NIV). In verses 25 and 64 Jesus' answer, su eipas, literally ‘you said’, is rendered ‘Thou hast said’ (KJV), ‘You have said so’ (ESV), or ‘You have said it yourself’ (BSB); David Catchpole (New Testament Studies, 1971) argued that it is an affirmation that puts the responsibility for the words on the questioner. In verse 41 ‘the flesh is weak’ (KJV, ESV) and ‘the body is weak’ (BSB) render sarx, which means human nature in its frailty rather than the body as opposed to the soul.

The quotation in verse 31 follows Mark in reading ‘I will strike the shepherd’, where the Hebrew of Zechariah 13:7 has the command “Strike the Shepherd”, addressed to the sword. The change makes explicit what the prophet implies, that God himself is the one who strikes.

teach.big: Jesus goes to his death knowingly and willingly, giving his body and blood for the forgiveness of sins and submitting to the Father's will, while those around him, friend and foe alike, show what human devotion and human failure look like.

outline.t: Jesus announces his death before his enemies plot it: the passion is his to give, not theirs to take.
Love for Jesus can look wasteful to the calculating, and he defends and remembers the extravagant devotion of a woman others dismissed.
Judas's bargain shows how cheaply Jesus can be sold by someone close to him.
Each disciple asks, Surely not I, and the question belongs in every heart, while Jesus both foreknows the betrayal and holds the betrayer responsible.
At the table Jesus gives himself: his body and his covenant blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins, with the promise of a feast to come.
Confident promises of loyalty are no match for the hour of testing, but Jesus has already promised to meet the scattered sheep in Galilee.
Jesus prays honestly and submits wholly, showing that faithful prayer can include both the plea for rescue and the yielding of the will.
Jesus refuses the sword and the angels, choosing the Father's way of suffering over force.
Under oath before the high priest, Jesus confesses who he is and claims the authority of the coming Son of Man, and is condemned for it.
Peter's collapse is complete, but his tears begin the road back to the risen Lord.

teach.pitfalls:
The first pitfall is to preach the chapter as a tragedy in which Jesus is a victim of circumstances. Matthew insists that he foresees, interprets, and freely accepts what happens, and a sermon that loses his agency loses the chapter's point. The opposite pitfall erases his humanity, treating Gethsemane as a performance by one who felt nothing. His sorrow is real, and the church has confessed that it is.

Verse 11 is often misused to excuse indifference to poverty. Jesus is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11, which goes on to command open-handed generosity to the poor, and his point is that this particular moment, before his burial, called for this particular act. With Judas, avoid two opposite errors: making him a cartoon villain with no resemblance to any disciple, when every disciple asked, Surely not I, and making him a hero or a helpless puppet of fate, which the text rejects with its woe in verse 24. Above all, avoid letting Judas, Caiaphas, or the council stand for the Jewish people; every person in the chapter, including all the disciples who fled, is Jewish, and the chapter's failures belong to humanity.

The Supper should not be taught as though one tradition's understanding of it were simply the text's meaning. Present the words themselves, note where the churches differ, and keep the chapter's own emphases: covenant, forgiveness, and the coming kingdom. Finally, do not preach verse 52 as if it settled every modern debate about war and policing; it rebukes a disciple's violence in defense of Jesus and has been read by pacifist and just war traditions in different ways.
teach.pastoral: This chapter meets people at some of life's deepest wounds. Those who have been betrayed by a close friend, a spouse, or a church leader will hear verses 21 to 25 and 47 to 50 with pain; Jesus knows that experience from the inside. Those who have failed badly, and especially those who failed someone they loved, will see themselves in Peter, and they need to hear that the story does not end at verse 75: the risen Jesus sends word to his brothers, Peter included (28:10). People in anguish or depression, or facing death, may find in Gethsemane permission to pray honestly for the cup to pass. And some come to the Lord's Table afraid that they are unworthy; the chapter's first communicants were about to deny and desert him, and he gave them the cup anyway, poured out for the forgiveness of sins.

hard.q: If Jesus' betrayal was foretold in Scripture, was Judas free, and is it just to condemn him?
hard.a:
The objection has a moral form and a historical one. The moral form asks how Judas can be blamed if the Son of Man must go just as it is written (verse 24) and if Jesus knew in advance what Judas would do; if the betrayal was necessary for salvation, Judas seems either a puppet or a benefactor. The second-century Gnostic Gospel of Judas, known to Irenaeus and recovered in the Codex Tchacos (published 2006), made Judas the one disciple who helped Jesus fulfill his mission, and Jorge Luis Borges's story Three Versions of Judas (1944) played with the same reversal. The historical form was put most sharply by the Jewish scholar Hyam Maccoby (Judas Iscariot and the Myth of Jewish Evil, 1992), who argued that Judas was largely a literary creation, a figure whose very name stood for the Jewish people and who carried the charge of betrayal onto them, with grievous results in Christian history. William Klassen (Judas: Betrayer or Friend of Jesus?, 1996) argued more modestly that the verb paradidōmi means only to hand over and that the earliest tradition did not call Judas a traitor.

Responses begin with the text. Matthew holds both truths in a single sentence: the Son of Man goes as it is written, but woe to the man by whom he is betrayed. Most Christian theologians, from Augustine through Thomas Aquinas and Calvin to modern Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant teaching, have held that God's foreknowledge and purpose do not remove human responsibility, since Judas acted from his own motives (verse 15 shows him asking for money) and God turned his evil to good, as with Joseph's brothers (Genesis 50:20, compare Acts 2:23). How divine purpose and human freedom fit together is itself a question Christians answer differently, from Calvinist to Arminian to Molinist accounts, and none declares Judas a mere instrument. Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2) gave Judas a long treatment as the rejected man for whom Christ was also handed over, leaving his final fate to God. On the historical question, most historians, including John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 3, 2001), judge that one of the Twelve handing Jesus over is too embarrassing to have been invented, since it reflected badly on Jesus' choice of disciples. Many Christian scholars also grant Maccoby's historical point about the misuse of Judas, and the churches' renunciation of the charge of collective Jewish guilt (Nostra Aetate, 1965) applies to Judas as to the crowd of 27:25. Judas was one Jew among twelve, and the other eleven, also Jews, are the ones who carried the gospel to the nations.

hard.q: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal, when John's Gospel seems to place the crucifixion on the day the lambs were killed?
hard.a:
The objection is that the Gospels contradict each other on the date of the crucifixion. Matthew, following Mark, presents the supper as a Passover meal eaten on the evening after the lambs were sacrificed (verses 17-19), so that Jesus dies on 15 Nisan, the feast day itself. John says that on the morning of the trial the priests had not yet eaten the Passover (John 18:28) and that Pilate sentenced Jesus on the day of Preparation for the Passover (John 19:14), so that Jesus dies on 14 Nisan as the lambs are slaughtered. The Babylonian Talmud also remembers that Yeshu was executed on the eve of Passover (b. Sanhedrin 43a). Many critical scholars conclude that one tradition has adjusted the date for theological reasons, either the Synoptic Gospels turning a farewell meal into a Passover or John moving the death to present Jesus as the Passover lamb (compare John 19:36).

Three kinds of answer have been offered. Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) argued at length that the meal had the marks of a Passover: it was eaten at night, inside Jerusalem, reclining, with wine, a dish for dipping, words interpreting the food, and a hymn at the end. Others, including many conservative harmonizers, argue that John's phrases refer to the other festival meals of the week and to the Friday of Passover week, so that John and the Synoptics agree. A third group appeals to different calendars: Annie Jaubert (1957) proposed that Jesus followed the priestly solar calendar known from Jubilees and Qumran and ate the meal on Tuesday evening, and Colin Humphreys (The Mystery of the Last Supper, 2011) proposed a Wednesday meal on an older lunar reckoning. Raymond Brown and others judge that Jesus held a farewell meal with Passover overtones the evening before the official Passover. No solution commands general agreement. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover, on a Friday, the day before the Sabbath, and that his death was understood in the light of the exodus, and the Supper carries that meaning on any of these reconstructions.

observe: What did the disciples say about the woman's act, and what three things did Jesus say in her defense?
What words does Jesus speak over the bread and over the cup, and what does he promise about the fruit of the vine?
Trace Peter's three denials. To whom does he speak each time, and how does his language change?
interpret: Why do you think Matthew notes that Judas called Jesus Rabbi while the other disciples called him Lord?
What does the cup mean in Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, and why might he have dreaded it so deeply?
Jesus could have called twelve legions of angels. What does his refusal show about the kind of Messiah he is?
apply: The woman's gift looked wasteful to others. What would it mean for you to give something costly to Christ that others might not understand?
Each disciple asked, Surely not I. Where are you most tempted to think that you could never fail Jesus?
How might Jesus' prayer, not as I will, but as You will, shape the way you pray about something you dread right now?
